# Skills for agents

<!-- GENERATED by scripts/docs/reference.ts. Do not edit; run `pnpm docs:reference`. -->

A skill is a short set of rules, with numbers, for one step of making a video: what to ask before building, where text may go at every aspect ratio, loudness and ducking, caption limits, sync tolerances, brand consistency and the checks before delivery.
Each rule comes from a published standard (EBU, ITU, WCAG, Netflix and BBC timed text) and says which tools and fields apply it here.
An agent that reads the skill for the step it is on makes fewer of the defaults that make a video look generic.

## Reading them

| Where | How |
| --- | --- |
| MCP | `get_skill` without `name` lists them; `get_skill { name }` returns one as Markdown. Resources `renderweld://skills` (the index) and `renderweld://skills/<name>`. |
| REST | `GET /v1/skills` (the list) and `GET /v1/skills/:name` (`text/markdown`). Both need the `read` scope. |
| Agent tools | `renderweld skills export <dir>` writes `<dir>/renderweld-<name>/SKILL.md` for each skill, the folder layout Claude Code (`.claude/skills/`), Codex and other agent tools load. `--prefix` changes the folder prefix; a changed file is kept unless `--force`. `renderweld skills list` prints them. |

The workflow guide (`renderweld://guide/workflow`, the `make_reel` prompt) starts with the brief and points to the skills.

## Adding your own

Set `skills.dir` (`RENDERWELD_SKILLS_DIR`) to a folder of skills: your house rules, or a skills pack. They are served beside the built-in ones, and one with a built-in's name replaces it.

- Each skill is `<name>.md` or `<name>/SKILL.md`, the Agent Skills format: front matter with `name` (lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, matching the file or folder name) and `description` (at most 1024 characters; say when to use it), `title` optional, then Markdown.
- At most 256 KiB a skill and 200 skills.
- The folder is read at start-up. A file that cannot be used stops the start with its name, so a broken pack is never served half-loaded.

```markdown
---
name: house-style
description: Our lower thirds, logo placement and words we never use. Use for every video for the Acme brand.
---
# House style

1. The logo sits bottom right, 4 % of the short side, on every scene.
```

<a id="video-brief"></a>

## Video brief

`video-brief`: Turn a request into a written brief before building anything, so the manifest comes from the user's answers, not from guesses. Use when a new video starts, or when its goal, platform or length changes.

**Use when:** a new video starts, or the goal, platform or length changes.
A model fills every gap you leave with a default, and defaults are what make
videos look generic. Ask, or write the default down and mark it assumed.

### Rules
1. Never infer the goal, audience, platform or length from style words
   ("modern", "engaging"). Ask, or state the default and label it *assumed*.
2. Ask the open questions in one message, at most about eight, each with a
   suggested default the user can accept with "yes":
   goal (one sentence: "after watching, <who> will <do what>"), audience and
   language, where it is posted (platform, organic or paid), size or sizes,
   length, tone (three adjectives, each turned into something measurable such
   as pace or colour), brand (logo, colours, fonts), the one call to action,
   captions (burned, sidecar file, both, which languages), voice (human or
   synthetic, accent, pace), music (licence source) and anything that must
   appear word for word.
3. Take sizes and limits from the platform's current spec, not from memory.
   Size is never assumed: if the user did not say, ask; there is no "usual"
   aspect ratio.
4. Every factual claim in the video traces to a source the user gave you;
   otherwise leave it out. Never invent numbers, quotes or testimonials.
5. Record the licence of every asset you add (music, fonts, footage, images,
   a voice or likeness). A cloned or synthetic voice of a real person needs
   that person's consent, from the user.
6. If the video shows realistic synthetic people or events, decide with the
   user how it will be disclosed on the platform it goes to.
7. List the deliverables: every size, language, caption file and cut-down.
8. Read the brief back as a short table and wait for an explicit yes before
   writing scenes. Keep open questions listed; do not resolve them yourself.

### In RenderWeld
- The `brief_intake` prompt asks the open questions in one message; use it.
- Store the answers in the manifest `brief`: `goal`, `audience`, `style`,
  `platform`, `targetSeconds`. `validate_project` warns when the total length
  is more than 10 % off `targetSeconds`.
- `brief.platform` changes the safe areas of tall frames (see
  `layout-and-type`). Extra sizes are `variants`; each may set its own
  `platform`.
- Asset licences go in `upload_asset` / `add_asset_from_url` (`license`);
  `validate_project` warns about assets without one.
- Captions: `update_captions { mode }`; voice: `generate_voice` needs the
  user's agreement to the cost (`acknowledgeCost: true`).

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- A silent default size and length nobody asked for.
- Tone words with no numbers behind them; invented statistics.
- Default "upbeat" music chosen without the user.

### Before you render
- [ ] Goal sentence, audience, platform, size(s), length and the call to action are the user's, or marked assumed and confirmed.
- [ ] Caption mode, voice and music decided with the user; every asset has a licence.
- [ ] Every claim has a source; disclosure decided where it applies.
- [ ] The user said yes to the brief.

### Sources
- OpenAI, Sora 2 prompting guide: unstated details are invented by the model (developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/sora/sora2_prompting_guide).
- US FTC, advertising substantiation policy (ftc.gov).
- YouTube and TikTok policies on labelling realistic synthetic content (support.google.com/youtube/answer/14328491; tiktok.com/transparency).

<a id="layout-and-type"></a>

## Layout and type

`layout-and-type`: Safe areas for every aspect ratio, type sizes relative to the frame, contrast, line length and lower thirds. Use whenever you place text, a logo or interface elements.

**Use when:** placing any text, logo or UI, at any size or aspect ratio.

### Rules
1. Keep text inside the title-safe area and important action inside
   action-safe. On 16:9, graphics-safe is 5 % from each edge and action-safe
   3.5 % (EBU R 95). Square and 4:5: keep text inside the central 90 % × 90 %.
2. Tall frames (9:16) on social platforms are covered by the app's own
   buttons, captions and account name. Use the platform's published overlay
   for the exact zones; when one video goes to several platforms, stay inside
   all of them. A conservative fallback for 1080×1920: about 14 % clear at
   the top, 35 % at the bottom and 6 % at each side.
3. Size type from the frame's height, not in fixed pixels: titles about
   4-9 % of the frame height, secondary text 2.5-4 %, nothing smaller than
   2.6 % of the shorter side. Check a copy scaled to 360 px wide: if you
   cannot read it there, it is too small for a phone.
4. Titles: at most two lines and about 37 characters a line. Avoid
   paragraphs on screen.
5. Contrast: at least 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for large text (WCAG 2.2,
   1.4.3), measured against the busiest frame behind it. Over video or
   photos, put the text on a solid box or a dark scrim.
6. One focal point per frame; at most two type families and three sizes per
   scene; no uppercase text with wide letter-spacing as decoration.
7. Use a grid: margins equal to the safe area, and recurring elements
   (lower thirds, captions, logo) in the same place in every scene.
8. A lower third sits inside the safe area and stays at least 0.5 s plus
   0.3 s per word. Captions move up while a lower third is on screen.
9. Wider than 16:9 (21:9): compose so the important part also works in a
   16:9 crop.
10. Re-lay out each size; never centre-crop one size into another.

### In RenderWeld
- `--rf-unit` is 1 % of the shorter side; size and space everything in it so
  scenes reflow for every output and variant.
- `--rf-safe-top/right/bottom/left` are the safe insets for this output and
  platform (`--rf-title-safe-*`, `--rf-action-safe-*` too); keep text inside
  them. `brief.platform` (or a variant's `platform`) switches the app-interface
  zone of tall frames on or off.
- Layout templates (`html-layout` and its twins on the other engines) give
  split screen, picture-in-picture, grids and a lower third that reflow for
  every size.
- Built-in templates fit text to their boxes; long text gets smaller, so
  keep it short instead of relying on the fit.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Text under the app's buttons or touching the frame edge.
- Gradient text, glows, stacked drop shadows, emoji used as icons.
- Five fonts; everything centred with no grid.

### Before you render
- [ ] Every size checked on a frame with the platform overlay in mind.
- [ ] Contrast measured on the worst frame; text readable at 360 px wide.
- [ ] Reading times met: on-screen text and captions at most 20 characters a second (see `captions-and-accessibility`).

### Sources
- EBU R 95, safe areas for 16:9 production (tech.ebu.ch/docs/r/r095.pdf); ITU-R BT.1848.
- W3C WCAG 2.2, success criterion 1.4.3 (w3.org/TR/WCAG22).
- BBC Subtitle Guidelines (line lengths and regions).
- TikTok, YouTube and Meta safe-zone overlays (ads.tiktok.com; services.google.com/fh/files/misc/universalsafezones-youtube.pdf).

<a id="sound-and-mix"></a>

## Sound and mix

`sound-and-mix`: Loudness targets, ducking, dialogue-to-music balance, sound-effect audibility, beat arithmetic and clean endings. Use when adding music, sound effects or voice to a video, and when reading the render's audio checks. (Which music and sound effects suit the video is the user's choice.)

**Use when:** adding or placing music, sound effects or voice, and when the
render reports audio issues. Which music and sound effects fit, and where
they go, is decided with the user; this skill is about levels and timing.

### Rules
1. Integrated loudness by destination (ITU-R BS.1770 measurement): web and
   social about -14 LUFS with true peak at or under -1 dBTP; European
   broadcast -23 LUFS, -1 dBTP (EBU R 128); US broadcast -24 LKFS (ATSC A/85).
   Deliver one target per file; variants of the same video match each other.
2. Speech must stay clearly above the music: keep the voice at least 7 dB
   above the bed, preferably 12 dB or more. Listeners, including hard-of-
   hearing listeners, rate the larger gap better.
3. Duck the music under speech: 12-20 dB lower; short attack (tens of
   milliseconds) and a release of a few hundred milliseconds; hold the duck
   through pauses shorter than about a second instead of pumping.
4. No sung lyrics under narration.
5. A sound effect lands on its picture event within ±1 frame; audio must
   never arrive more than about 45 ms before the picture (ITU-R BT.1359).
6. Each sound effect must be audible over the bed in its first half second.
   One that sits under the music is noise, not design: raise it, lower the
   music, or remove it.
7. Beat arithmetic: frames per beat = fps × 60 ÷ BPM (120 BPM at 30 fps is
   15 frames). Compute each beat frame from its index and round once; put
   cuts on beats and scene changes on phrase boundaries (4 or 8 bars).
8. Music ends on the end of a phrase, or fades over at least a second. Never
   stop it dead at the last frame.
9. Never clip: if the render reports a peak-limited mix, lower the loudest
    sounds (usually sound effects) rather than pushing the limiter.

### In RenderWeld
- `audio.loudness` picks the preset: `social` (-14 LUFS, -2 dBTP ceiling for
  the AAC encode), `broadcast-ebu`, `broadcast-atsc`, `podcast` or `off`.
  The finished file is measured; misses are in `audio.qa.issues`
  (`render.audio.loudnessQa` decides warn or fail).
- Ducking: `audio.music.ducking: true` or `{ depthDb, attackMs, releaseMs,
  thresholdDb }` (defaults 18 dB, 120 ms, 400 ms, -40 dB). It needs a voice.
- Balance: each track's `volume`, then bus gains `audio.gainDb.{voice,music,sfx}`.
  Fades: `audio.music.fadeInSeconds` and `fadeOutSeconds`.
- Sound effects: `audio.sfx: [{ asset, atFrame, volume }]`; `atFrame` is the
  frame of the picture event.
- Turn buses off for one render without editing the project:
  `render_project { audio: { music: false } }`, or `mute: true`.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Music louder than the voice; a hard stop at the end.
- Sound effects you can see but not hear; clipped peaks.

### Before you render
- [ ] Loudness preset matches the destination; variants share it.
- [ ] Ducking on wherever music plays under speech.
- [ ] Every sound effect on its frame and audible; music ends on a phrase or fades.

### Sources
- EBU R 128 (tech.ebu.ch/docs/r/r128-2014.pdf); ITU-R BS.1770; ATSC A/85.
- Spotify loudness normalisation (artists.spotify.com/help/article/loudness-normalization).
- ITU-R BT.1359 (detectability of audio ahead of video).
- Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research, 2026, on dialogue-to-background ratios (pubs.asha.org/doi/10.1044/2026_JSLHR-25-00127).
- Audacity Auto Duck defaults (manual.audacityteam.org/man/auto_duck.html).

<a id="captions-and-accessibility"></a>

## Captions and accessibility

`captions-and-accessibility`: Caption length, reading speed, timing, placement, line breaks, sound descriptions, audio description and flashing limits. Use for any video with speech, and any video with flashing or high-contrast patterns.

**Use when:** a video has speech, or contains flashes, strobes or striped
patterns.

### Rules
1. Every video with speech has captions (WCAG 2.2, 1.2.2). Give a sidecar
   file (WebVTT or SRT) where the platform takes one; burn them in as well for
   social video that autoplays without sound. Long-form video is never
   burned-in only.
2. Line length at most 42 characters (stricter guides use 32); about 25 on
   tall frames. At most two lines on landscape and square frames.
3. Reading speed at most 20 characters a second for adults, 17 for children.
4. Each caption stays at least 5/6 s and at most 7 s, with a gap of at least
   two frames between captions; snap starts and ends to nearby cuts.
5. Sync: a caption appears with its speech, not before it by more than a
   moment, and never trails it by more than about 1.5 s.
6. Break lines at natural points: after punctuation, before conjunctions and
   prepositions; never split an article from its noun or a first name from a
   last name; the lower line may be longer.
7. Placement: bottom centre by default; move up for on-screen text, lower
   thirds and faces; on tall frames keep clear of the app's interface.
8. Style: a box or a strong outline behind the text, at least 4.5:1
   contrast. Identify speakers with labels or consistent colours.
9. Hard-of-hearing captions (SDH): speaker names and sounds in lowercase
   brackets ("[door slams]"), music described by mood; describe what is
   heard, not what is seen.
10. When the picture carries information that the audio does not, give an
    audio description (WCAG 1.2.5), or write the narration so it describes
    what matters.
11. Flashing: no more than three flashes in any one second, unless the
    flashing area is small (under about 25 % of a 10° field of view). Red
    flashes count separately and are worse. Avoid high-contrast stripes over
    large areas and long flashing sequences altogether (WCAG 2.2, 2.3.1).
12. Test anything that flashes with a photosensitivity analyser before
    publishing.

### In RenderWeld
- `captions.mode`: `off`, `burned`, `sidecar` or `both`; override for one
  render with `render_project { captions }`. Sidecars are SRT, WebVTT and ASS.
- Cues come from voice word timings (`generate_voice`), local speech-to-text
  (`transcribe_captions`), `import_captions` (SRT or WebVTT) or your own text.
- Caption QA follows the rules above (42 characters, 32 on portrait, two
  lines, 20 characters a second, 5/6 s to 7 s, two-frame gaps) and is
  reported by `get_captions` and in the render; fix every issue.
- Show the user the cue texts and times, ask for approval, then
  `update_captions { approve: true }`; never assume approval.
- Several languages: `update_captions { language, cues }`; `burnLanguage`
  picks the one burned in. Audio description: cues with `kind: "description"`
  (a WebVTT sidecar, never burned).
- Caption style (font, size, colours, box, outline) comes from the theme.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Bouncing word-by-word captions with emoji; captions over faces or the product.
- Blocks of uppercase text; no sound labels.
- Strobing "energy" transitions.

### Before you render
- [ ] Caption QA clean; names spelled correctly; the user approved the cues.
- [ ] Placement checked on every size; nothing under the platform interface.
- [ ] Audio description decided; no flashing over the limits.

### Sources
- Netflix Timed Text Style Guide and timing guidelines (partnerhelp.netflixstudios.com; backlothelp.netflix.com).
- BBC Subtitle Guidelines (bbc.co.uk/accessibility/forproducts/guides/subtitles).
- DCMP Captioning Key (dcmp.org/learn/captioningkey).
- US FCC caption quality standards, 47 CFR 79.1.
- W3C WCAG 2.2: 1.2.2, 1.2.5, 1.4.3, 2.3.1 (w3.org/TR/WCAG22).
- ITU-R BT.1702 (photosensitive epilepsy).

<a id="av-sync"></a>

## Audio and video sync

`av-sync`: Tolerances for sound against picture, frame arithmetic, aligning visuals to narration and beats, and checking the result. Use when timing visuals to voice, music or sound effects, and when checking a render.

**Use when:** timing a visual to a word, a beat or a sound, and when checking
a render.

### Rules
1. Tolerances: sound ahead of the picture is noticed at about 45 ms and
   unacceptable at about 90 ms; sound behind is noticed at about 125 ms and
   unacceptable at about 185 ms (ITU-R BT.1359). Aim for zero: audio never
   more than one frame early or three frames late.
2. Keep the timeline in frames, at a constant frame rate, with 48 kHz audio.
   Convert seconds to frames once, from absolute times.
3. A visual that a word names appears at the start of that word, or up to
   about 0.2 s before it, never noticeably after. People tolerate the
   picture leading the sound far better than the reverse.
4. A bullet point appears at the start of its phrase and stays through the
   sentence.
5. Beat frames: round(index × fps × 60 ÷ BPM + offset). Cut on the beat
   frame or one frame before it.
6. After rendering, measure: voice onsets against caption cues and visual
   events, and report the offset in milliseconds.

### In RenderWeld
- Every render checks that audio starts at 0 and that audio and video last
  the same within one frame (`checks.avSync`); a mismatch fails the render.
- `generate_voice` stores word timestamps; use them to place scene starts,
  bullet points and caption cues instead of estimating.
- Voice placement: `audio.voice.startFrame`; sound effects:
  `audio.sfx[].atFrame`. Both are frames, so compute them with rule 2.
- `validate_project` errors when a voice or sound effect starts after the end.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Narration describing a feature while the previous picture is still up.
- Cuts half a beat late; sound effects trailing the picture.

### Before you render
- [ ] Word timestamps used for every narration-driven visual.
- [ ] Beat grid computed if cutting to music.
- [ ] `checks.avSync` passes; measured offsets within one frame.

### Sources
- ITU-R BT.1359-1, relative timing of sound and vision (itu.int).
- EBU R 37 (broadcast chain targets).
- van Wassenhove et al. (2007), temporal window of audiovisual speech integration (doi.org/10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2006.01.001).

<a id="brand-consistency"></a>

## Brand consistency

`brand-consistency`: Logo rules, colour tokens, type, motion and sound kept identical across scenes, sizes and a series. Use for any branded video, template or series.

**Use when:** the video belongs to a brand, or is part of a series.

### Rules
1. Collect the brand kit before designing: logo files (light, dark and
   single-colour; vector where possible), clear space and minimum size,
   colours with approved text-on-background pairs, fonts licensed for video,
   motion style, sound logo, tone of voice and anything banned.
2. Never stretch, rotate, recolour or add effects to a logo, and never
   animate it unless the kit supplies an animated version.
3. Respect the kit's clear space (often a letter height or half the logo's
   height) and minimum size.
4. The logo keeps the same corner and size in every scene and every size,
   inside the safe area. An end card with logo and call to action holds at
   least 2 s.
5. In ads, show the brand early (within about 5 s), but do not open with a
   logo sting before the subject.
6. Colours come only from the kit's tokens: neutral backgrounds, one accent,
   every text colour checked for contrast against its background.
7. One motion style (fast and subtle, or expressive) with a fixed set of
   durations and curves; the same transition family across a series.
8. One music family, one sound logo and one voice per language for a series.
9. Images keep one grade, one lighting logic and one illustration style.
10. Build reusable scenes from the kit's values; never hard-code a colour or
    font that should come from the brand. Version the kit.

### In RenderWeld
- A theme is the brand kit in the renderer: `create_theme` with
  `colors` (background, surface, text, mutedText, accent, accent2),
  `fontFamily`, `headingWeight`, `motionSpeed` and caption style; apply it
  with `set_theme`. Templates and html scenes read the same tokens
  (`--rf-bg`, `--rf-text`, `--rf-muted`, `--rf-accent`, `--rf-font`,
  `--rf-heading-weight`, `--rf-speed`).
- Fonts: upload the font files as assets and name the family in the theme;
  they render offline in every engine and in burned captions.
- Logos: upload as assets (vector SVG is stored sanitised) and place them in
  the same pane or corner in every scene.
- Every size is a `variant` of the same project, so the brand stays identical
  across sizes.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Purple-to-blue gradients, glass blobs, neon glows.
- A pulsing or spinning logo; colours that are not in the kit.
- Stock footage of people high-fiving.

### Before you render
- [ ] Logo clear space and size checked; same position in every scene.
- [ ] Only theme colours used; contrast checked.
- [ ] Motion and sound consistent with the rest of the series.

### Sources
- W3C WCAG 2.2, 1.4.3 contrast.
- IBM Carbon motion: productive and expressive motion (carbondesignsystem.com).
- Google ad creative guidance on early branding (support.google.com/google-ads/answer/14783551).

<a id="review-and-qa"></a>

## Review and QA

`review-and-qa`: The professional editor's pass before a video is called final: technical checks, frames to look at, creative checks, findings and variants. Use before any render is delivered, and after any change to a delivered video.

**Use when:** before you call a render final, and after every change.
The renderer checks the file; you check whether the video works.

### Rules
1. Each output matches its spec: size, aspect ratio and a constant frame
   rate; duration within one frame of the plan.
2. Loudness and true peak on target; sound in sync within a frame; no
   flashing over the limits (see `captions-and-accessibility`).
3. Captions pass their checks, names are spelled right, and the user
   approved the cues.
4. Automatic checks: the first frame is not empty; no stretch over about 3 s
   without change; no text smaller than 2.6 % of the short side; no line on
   screen too briefly to read; a video over 15 s is not silent unless that
   was asked for.
5. Look at frames, not only reports: each scene at its start and middle,
   the frames on both sides of every cut, and the last frame, at phone size
   (360 px wide).
6. Creative checks: the subject is clear from the first frame; one message
   and one call to action; with text and sound off, the pictures still tell
   the story; a stranger could describe each key frame in one sentence.
7. Watch every generated clip (footage from a media provider) at full size
   for artefacts: warped hands and faces, text that changes from frame to
   frame, objects that appear, vanish or pass through each other.
8. Every claim traces to the brief's sources; every asset has its licence;
   disclosure is applied where needed.
9. Write findings ranked P0 (must fix), P1 (should fix), P2 (nice to have),
   each with the time, the problem, the exact change, and what to keep. No
   scores.
10. Variants: re-lay out each size instead of cropping; an A/B test changes
    one thing (the opening, the call to action or the thumbnail).
11. Name outputs so they sort and explain themselves, e.g.
    `project_v003_9x16_en_hookB.mp4`; keep the project version each render
    was made from.

### In RenderWeld
- `validate_project`: errors block the render; read every warning.
- `preview_scene`: a low-resolution render of one scene or the whole
  project (per variant) to look at before the final render.
- `get_render_output`: `checks` (metadata, decode, duration, avSync,
  loudness), `audio.qa.issues`, caption QA, the poster image, the storage
  location and a download link.
- `get_captions`: cue QA. `list_project_versions`: what changed; each render
  records the project version it was made from.
- The `review_reel` prompt walks through this checklist with the manifest
  and the validation report.
- Every size is a `variant`: `render_project { variants: [...] }` renders
  them in one call.

### Signs of a generic, machine-made video
- Never watched at phone size; auto-crops cutting off heads.
- Juddering from a frame-rate mismatch; loudness that differs between variants.

### Before you deliver
- [ ] Technical: spec, checks, loudness, sync, captions, flashing.
- [ ] Frames: start, middle, cuts, last frame, at phone size.
- [ ] Creative: subject from frame one, one message, one call to action.
- [ ] Findings written as P0/P1/P2 and all P0s fixed.
